common_name: African Milk Tree (Cathedral Cactus, Friendship Cactus)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings (allow the cut end to callus for several days before potting, since the latex sap otherwise inhibits rooting) or plant container specimens in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright light with some direct sun; African milk tree has no frost tolerance and is grown outdoors year-round only in zone 10-11, elsewhere as a container houseplant. CAUTION: the milky latex sap is a severe skin and eye irritant — wear gloves and eye protection when handling or pruning.

directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun, in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only after the soil has dried out. African milk tree is a fast-growing, cactus-like succulent shrub from Central Africa with tall, upright, triangular, ridged stems edged in small paired thorns and tiny leaves along the ridges; the widely sold 'Rubra' form has deep burgundy-red coloring that intensifies in strong light. Stems branch readily from the base and from pruning cuts, quickly producing a dense, candelabra-like clump that can eventually reach several feet tall indoors. Handle only with gloves and eye protection, since like other Euphorbias it exudes a milky latex sap when cut that is a potent skin and eye irritant and toxic if ingested; keep well away from children and pets. Repot every couple of years into fresh, fast-draining mix and prune to control height, using the resulting cuttings to propagate new plants after a callusing period.

common_name: Crested Elkhorn Euphorbia (Coral Cactus, Frilled Fan Euphorbia)

planting.note: Plant grafted specimens in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright light with some direct sun; the crested form is a mutation that cannot photosynthesize efficiently enough to grow on its own roots and is sold grafted onto a vigorous Euphorbia or Hylocereus rootstock, which handles all water and nutrient uptake.

directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun, in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering sparingly and only once the soil has dried out. This novelty succulent is a fan-shaped, crested (cristate) mutation of Euphorbia lactea that grows in wavy, undulating, coral-like ridges rather than the species' normal upright triangular stems, and the pale outer growth is often further dyed pink, yellow, or orange by growers for a more colorful effect, though the natural crest is pale green mottled with white marbling. Because the crested tissue lacks sufficient chlorophyll and vigor to sustain itself, plants are almost always grafted onto a sturdy green rootstock such as Euphorbia neriifolia or a hardy dragon fruit cactus, visible as a distinct stem below the frilled crest. Handle with gloves and eye protection, since the plant still exudes the caustic milky latex typical of Euphorbia when cut or damaged, and watch the graft union for rot, which is the most common cause of failure in cultivation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown specimens in spring into very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in bright light with some direct sun; Euphorbia obesa is dioecious (separate male and female plants), and since it is a slow-growing, vulnerable South African species, only purchase nursery-propagated plants rather than wild-collected material.

directions: Grow in bright light with some direct sun, in very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix, watering sparingly and only once the soil has dried out completely. Baseball plant is a slow-growing South African succulent whose nearly spherical, leafless, ribbed stem is patterned with alternating bands of green and grayish-purple that closely mimic the stitching of a baseball, an appearance that has made it a favorite novelty succulent for collectors and windowsill growers alike. Unlike spiny cacti, it is entirely unarmed but still exudes a caustic milky latex when cut or damaged, so handle with care and wash off any sap contacting skin immediately. Its extremely slow growth means offsets and new plants are usually grown from seed rather than cuttings, and mature plants eventually elongate slightly from the classic ball shape as they age. Give excellent drainage above all else, since overwatering and cool, wet conditions are by far the most common causes of rot in cultivation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
